summary: This unit teaches you to choose and use electrical measuring instruments safely and correctly. You will learn the quantities and units, Ohm's law and the power formula, and how to measure voltage, current and resistance with a multimeter and a clamp meter. You will also learn to carry out continuity, polarity and insulation resistance tests on dead circuits, read analogue and digital displays, look after and calibrate instruments, and record results properly.

blocks.p: An electrician measures all the time: to check a supply, to prove a circuit dead, to test new work before it is connected and to find faults. A measurement is only useful if the right instrument is used, on the right setting, connected the right way, and if the reading is understood and recorded. A wrong setting can destroy a meter or cause an arc flash in your face. This unit is for Level 2 trainees, who measure on low-voltage training boards and on circuits that are isolated and proved dead, under supervision.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Use quantities, units and Ohm's law
Name volts, amps, ohms, watts and hertz; change units such as mA to A; use I = V ÷ R and P = V × I to work out and check readings.
Pick a multimeter, clamp meter, insulation tester, continuity tester, energy meter or other instrument for the job, with a suitable CAT rating.
Inspect the case, leads and probes, check the battery and fuses, and check the meter on a known value.
Set the right function and range, connect the meter in parallel across the part, and read and record the value.
Switch off, break the circuit, connect the meter in series in the right socket, then switch on and read; or use a clamp meter round one conductor.
Measure only on dead circuits, null the leads, and judge whether a reading shows an unbroken path.
Check that switches are in the line conductor, and test insulation between conductors with an insulation tester, safely.
Read digital displays, signs and symbols, and analogue scales without parallax error.
Switch off, clean, store and calibrate instruments, replace fuses with the exact type, and take faulty ones out of use.
Write each result straight away with its unit, and check and report readings that are not as expected.

blocks.note: Jamaica's supply is **110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz**. At Level 2 you measure on low-voltage training boards (such as 12 V DC) and on circuits that are isolated and proved dead. Measurements on live mains are made only by qualified, authorised people, with instruments and PPE suited to the job.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order. Work through each example with a calculator. Then try the practice test and read every explanation, even when you get the answer right. Your instructor will show you the Centre's own meters, whose dials and sockets may differ a little from the ones described here: always read the maker's instructions.

head: Quantity
Symbol in formulas
Unit
Unit symbol
What it means
rows: The flow of electric charge through a circuit.
How much a material or part opposes current.
How fast energy is used or delivered.
Power used over time: what the electricity bill charges for.
The number of cycles per second of an alternating current.

ul: **DC (direct current)** flows in one direction only. Batteries, solar panels and most electronic circuits give DC. On a meter it is shown by a straight line, often with a dashed line under it (V⎓ or A⎓).
**AC (alternating current)** changes direction many times a second. The JPS supply is AC at 50 Hz: 50 complete cycles every second. On a meter AC is shown by a wavy line (V~ or A~).

A mains voltage of 110 V or 220 V is its **RMS** (effective) value: the steady DC voltage that would give the same heating effect. The voltage actually swings to a peak of about 1.4 times this (about 156 V on a 110 V supply) twice in every cycle.
mA to A: divide by 1,000. A to mA: multiply by 1,000. For example, 0.08 A = 80 mA.
kΩ to Ω: multiply by 1,000. MΩ to kΩ: multiply by 1,000. For example, 0.5 MΩ = 500 kΩ = 500,000 Ω.
Always check the prefix on the display: 1.5 kΩ and 1.5 MΩ are a thousand times different.

blocks.p: **Ohm's law** links voltage, current and resistance: the current is the voltage divided by the resistance. Cover the quantity you want in the triangle V over I × R:

head: To find
Formula
Example
rows: A 24 Ω lamp on 12 V: I = 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5 A
0.25 A through a 40 Ω resistor: V = 0.25 × 40 = 10 V

head: To find
Formula
Example
rows: A 1,100 W microwave on 110 V: I = 1,100 ÷ 110 = 10 A

blocks.p: **Energy** = power × time. A 2 kW water heater that runs for 3 hours uses 2 × 3 = **6 kWh**. The JPS meter counts kilowatt-hours, and the bill charges for each one.

blocks.note: Use Ohm's law to check your readings. If a lamp is rated 12 V 6 W, it should draw about 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 A. A reading of 5 A or 0.05 A tells you that something is wrong: the setting, the range, the connection or the circuit.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Hot and cold resistance.** The filament of an ordinary lamp has a much higher resistance when it is glowing than when it is cold: often ten times or more. So a resistance reading taken on a cold lamp will be far lower than V ÷ I worked out while it is lit. Heating elements made of resistance wire change much less.

head: Feature
Series
Parallel
rows: One after another, in a single loop
Side by side, each across the same two points
Divides: the branch currents **add up** to the total
Divides: the voltages across the parts **add up** to the supply voltage
Add them: R = R1 + R2 + R3
A switch and fuse in series with a load; old decorative light strings
Lights and outlets in a building: every load gets the full supply voltage

ul: **Two equal resistors in parallel:** half of one. Two 30 Ω in parallel = 15 Ω.
**Two different resistors in parallel:** product over sum. 20 Ω and 30 Ω: (20 × 30) ÷ (20 + 30) = 600 ÷ 50 = 12 Ω.
**More in parallel:** 1 ÷ R = 1 ÷ R1 + 1 ÷ R2 + 1 ÷ R3, then turn the answer upside down.

blocks.h: Worked example: two lamps on a 12 V board

blocks.p: Two identical lamps, each 24 Ω when lit, on a 12 V DC supply. (Real lamps change resistance with brightness, so measured values will differ a little.)

blocks.note: In the practical you measure these values and then compare them with what Ohm's law predicts. Small differences are normal. A large difference means a wrong setting, a poor connection or a fault: find out which before you write it down.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Instrument
What it measures
Notes
rows: Voltage, current and resistance, often continuity and more
The everyday instrument. Must be set correctly for each measurement.
Used only on dead circuits; uses its own battery.
Very small resistances, such as a grounding conductor
Gives a steady test current and reads to 0.01 Ω.
The resistance of insulation, in megohms (MΩ)
Makes its own high DC test voltage, such as 250 V, 500 V or 1,000 V. Dead circuits only.
Jaws go round one conductor; most also measure voltage and resistance through leads.
The instrument for proving a circuit dead.
The JPS meter at a building; sub-meters on circuits.
Also built into some clamp meters and energy monitors.
Speed of a shaft in revolutions per minute (rpm)
Contact type, or optical with reflective tape.
The shape of a voltage as it changes with time (the waveform)
Used in electronics; shows, for example, the 50 Hz sine wave of the mains.

head: Feature
Analogue (needle) meter
Digital meter
rows: A needle moving over printed scales
Shows a value rising or falling at a glance
Useful for watching a changing value
Some types work without a battery for voltage and current
Shows a minus sign if the leads are reversed on DC
Often has continuity beep, hold and other functions
Several scales: easy to read the wrong one
Parallax error if you look from the side
Must be zeroed before measuring resistance
Needs a battery; a weak one can give wrong readings
Numbers jump about on a changing value
Harder to see a slow trend

blocks.p: Mains supplies carry short, very high voltage spikes, for example from lightning or switching. A meter's **CAT rating** tells you where in an installation it can safely be used, because the closer you are to the supply, the bigger the spikes. Each rating comes with a voltage, such as **CAT III 600 V**.

head: Category
Where
Examples
rows: The service drop, the meter, the main breaker
Panels, breakers, fixed wiring, permanently connected motors and air-conditioners
Appliances, portable tools, the outlets' loads
Circuits not connected to the mains
Protected electronics, low-voltage training boards, battery circuits

ul: Choose a meter, and leads, rated for the **highest category and voltage** where you will use it. A CAT III 600 V meter can be used in CAT II and CAT I places, but a CAT II meter must not be used at a panel.
The rating of the whole set is that of its lowest-rated part: CAT II leads on a CAT III meter make a CAT II set.
Probes should have **finger guards** and shrouded tips, with only a short length of metal showing (often 4 mm or less, or with tip caps fitted).

flow: What must I measure, and is it AC or DC?
About what size do I expect, and what range covers it?
Is the circuit live or dead? (Resistance, continuity and insulation tests: dead only)
Where in the installation am I? Pick a suitable CAT and voltage rating
Is the instrument in date for calibration, undamaged and working?

sections.title: The multimeter: settings, sockets and readings

head: Symbol
Function
rows: V⎓ (or VDC): V with a straight line
Continuity: the meter beeps when the resistance is low
Switches the meter off and saves the battery

head: Socket
Which lead
Used for
rows: Small currents, usually up to a few hundred milliamps, through a small internal fuse
Larger currents, through a high-energy fuse; often only for a short time

blocks.note: **The red lead in a current socket turns the meter into almost a short circuit.** If it is then touched across a supply, a large current flows: the fuse blows at best, and at worst the meter bursts in an arc flash. After every current measurement, put the red lead back in the V Ω socket and turn the dial away from amps.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: An **auto-ranging** meter picks the range for you; a **manual** meter has several ranges for each function, such as 200 mV, 2 V, 20 V, 200 V and 600 V.
On a manual meter, if you do not know the size of the value, start on the **highest range** and step down until you get a clear reading. Starting too low can overload the meter.
The best range is the lowest one that is still higher than the value: 12 V is read best on the 20 V range, not the 200 V range.
Never turn the dial while the probes are connected to a circuit.

head: You see
It means
rows: Over the range: the value is too big for this range, or, on resistance and continuity, the path is open (broken)
A minus sign before a DC reading
The leads are the wrong way round; the size of the reading is still right
mV, kΩ, MΩ, mA beside the number
The prefix: check it every time
The meter's battery is low; readings may be wrong. Replace it before going on
The display is frozen on the last reading
A changing value or a poor contact; hold the probes firmly and wait for it to settle

blocks.p: **Resolution** is the smallest step the display can show. On a 20 V range a typical display shows 12.47 V, a resolution of 0.01 V. On the 200 V range it shows 12.5 V, a resolution of 0.1 V. That is why the lowest suitable range gives the most detail.
An analogue meter has several printed scales. You read the scale whose end figure matches, or divides easily into, the range you have selected, then multiply if needed.

ul: **Reading = (scale reading ÷ scale full value) × range.** On the 0–250 V range, a needle at 4.4 on the 0–10 scale reads 4.4 ÷ 10 × 250 = **110 V**.
On the 0–50 V range, a needle half-way across reads 25 V.
Look **straight at the needle**, with one eye, so that it covers its own reflection in the mirror strip. Looking from one side gives a **parallax error**.
The **ohms scale** runs backwards (0 Ω at the right, ∞ at the left) and is crowded at the left end. Choose an ohms range that puts the needle near the middle.
Before measuring resistance, touch the probes together and turn the **zero-adjust** knob until the needle reads 0 Ω. Do this again each time you change the ohms range.
With the meter switched off and nothing connected, the needle should rest on zero. If not, set it with the small screw under the needle (mechanical zero).

blocks.h: Measuring voltage: the meter goes in parallel

blocks.p: Voltage is the difference between two points, so the voltmeter is connected **across** the part, in parallel with it. A voltmeter has a very high resistance, so it takes almost no current and does not change the circuit.

flow: Check the meter, leads and probes for damage
Black lead in COM, red lead in V Ω
Set DC or AC volts, and a range higher than the expected value
Hold the probes behind the finger guards
Touch black to the negative (or neutral) side and red to the positive (or line) side
Read the display when it is steady
Record the value with its unit; remove the probes; switch off

head: Measurement on a 12 V DC board
What it tells you
rows: Whether the supply is at its rated voltage. A fully charged 12 V lead-acid battery at rest reads about 12.6–12.8 V; about 12.0 V or less means it is well run down (check the maker's table).
Across each lamp in a series circuit
How the supply voltage is shared. The lamp voltages add up to the supply voltage.
Across each lamp in a parallel circuit
Each should read the full supply voltage.
Across a closed switch or a good fuse
Close to 0 V: little voltage is lost across a good connection.
Across an open switch or a blown fuse in a working circuit
The full supply voltage: the break has the whole voltage across it.

blocks.h: Measuring current: the meter goes in series

blocks.p: Current is the flow **through** a part, so the ammeter must be put **into** the circuit, in series, so that all the current flows through it. An ammeter has a very low resistance, so that it does not reduce the current.

flow: Switch off the circuit
Set the dial to DC or AC amps
Black lead in COM; red lead in the 10 A socket if you are not sure of the size
Open the circuit at one point, for example by taking one wire off a lamp terminal
Connect the meter into the gap: red to the side from the supply's positive, black towards the load
Switch on and read; if the reading is small, switch off and move to the mA socket and a lower range
Switch off, remove the meter and reconnect the wire
Put the red lead back in V Ω and turn the dial off amps

blocks.note: Never connect an ammeter across a supply or across a part, the way you connect a voltmeter. With almost no resistance, it short-circuits whatever it is placed across.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A clamp meter measures current by sensing the **magnetic field** round a conductor that carries it. The circuit does not have to be switched off or broken. Most clamp meters measure AC current; some, with a different sensor, also measure DC.

ul: Set the dial to AC amps (A~) for a mains circuit.
Open the jaws and close them round **one conductor only**, such as the line conductor, with the jaws fully shut. Centre the conductor in the jaws if you can.

If the line and neutral are both inside the jaws, their currents are equal and opposite, their fields cancel and the meter reads about **zero**. A flexible cord must be split out, or measured with a line-splitter adaptor.
Keep your hand behind the guard on the clamp body, and never touch bare parts.
At the Centre, clamp readings on mains circuits are taken only on equipment the instructor has set up for it.

blocks.p: **Example.** A clamp round the line conductor of a 220 V, 2.2 kW water heater should read about 2,200 ÷ 220 = 10 A. A reading of about 10 A shows the heater is working at its rating; a much lower reading points to a fault, a low supply voltage or the wrong element, and 0 A while the thermostat is calling for heat means no current is flowing at all.

blocks.note: **Every test in this section is done on a dead circuit.** These instruments send their own current or voltage through the circuit. Any outside voltage can damage them and gives false readings, and the insulation tester's own voltage can give you a shock. Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead first, or work on a board that is not connected to any supply.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Isolate and prove dead, or take the part out of the circuit
Disconnect at least one end of the part, so that other parts in parallel do not change the reading
Black lead in COM, red in V Ω; set the dial to Ω
Touch the probes together: note the lead resistance (digital) or zero the needle (analogue)
Hold the probes firmly on the two ends, fingers off the metal tips
Read when steady, check the prefix (Ω, kΩ or MΩ) and take away the lead resistance if it matters
Compare with the expected value

ul: Keep your fingers off the probe tips and the part: your body is a resistance in parallel, and it lowers high readings.
**OL** on a resistance range means the value is higher than the range can show, or the path is open.
A reading of almost 0 Ω across a part that should have resistance, such as a heater element, suggests a short circuit.

blocks.p: A continuity test checks that a conductor has an **unbroken path** from one end to the other. On a multimeter's continuity setting the meter beeps when the resistance is below a low value set by the maker (often a few tens of ohms). For grounding conductors and other installation tests, a low-resistance ohmmeter is used, because it reads small values accurately.

ul: **Null the leads** first: touch them together and use the meter's null or zero button, or write down the lead resistance and take it away from each reading.
To test a long conductor, link it at the far end to another conductor (or use a long 'wander' lead), and measure the loop from the near end.
For short runs of installation cable, a good conductor reads well under 1 Ω. A high reading or OL means a break or a loose or dirty terminal.
Check the **grounding conductor** to every metal box, fitting and outlet ground terminal, because it must carry fault current.

blocks.p: **Example.** The leads read 0.3 Ω when touched together. A grounding conductor run reads 0.8 Ω including the leads. Its own resistance is 0.8 − 0.3 = **0.5 Ω**.
Polarity tests check that conductors are connected to the right terminals. They are done on the dead circuit with a continuity tester.

ul: Every **switch must be in the line (hot) conductor**, never in the neutral. A switch in the neutral turns the lamp off but leaves the lamp holder live, so someone changing a lamp could get a shock.
In a screw-type lamp holder, the **centre contact goes to the switched line** and the outer screw shell to the neutral, because the shell is easier to touch.

In a standard 110 V outlet of the US type used in Jamaica, the **narrow slot** (brass screw) is line, the **wide slot** (silver screw) is neutral and the **round or D-shaped hole** (green screw) is ground.
Check that the grounding conductor is connected to every metal box and fitting.

blocks.p: Insulation resistance tests check that the insulation between conductors, and between each conductor and ground, is sound, so that current cannot leak through it. Damaged or damp insulation causes shocks, fires and tripping. The insulation tester makes its own **high DC test voltage**. For 110/220 V circuits **500 V DC** is common; your instructor will give the test voltage to use.

flow: Isolate, lock off and prove the circuit dead
Remove lamps, unplug appliances and disconnect equipment the test voltage could damage (electronic switches, dimmers, LED drivers, GFCIs, surge protectors)
Close the switches so that every part of the circuit is tested
Check the tester: leads joined should read 0; leads apart should read the top value
Warn others and keep everyone off the circuit
Test between line and neutral, line and ground, and neutral and ground
Keep your hands off the conductors and probe tips during each test
Let the circuit discharge (most testers do it automatically) before touching it
Record each result; reconnect the lamps and equipment

ul: Good insulation gives a **high reading in megohms**. A new circuit often reads hundreds of megohms, or more than the tester's top value (shown as '>' or OL).

Many test standards accept no less than about 1 MΩ on circuits like these. Any reading much lower than similar circuits should be investigated: your instructor will give the pass value the Centre uses.
A lamp left in its holder, or an appliance left plugged in, connects line to neutral through its filament or circuit, so that pair reads very low. Remove it and test again.
A low reading between a conductor and ground usually means damaged insulation, for example a cable nicked by a screw, crushed in a box or wet.

blocks.note: The insulation tester's test voltage, such as 500 V, can give a painful shock, and long cables can store a charge after the test. Never touch the conductors or probe tips during a test, and let the circuit discharge before you touch it.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Use an instrument with a CAT and voltage rating suitable for where you are measuring, and leads of the same rating.
Before use, check the case, leads, probes and plugs for cracks, bare metal, burns or loose parts. Damaged leads are taken out of use.
Check the battery and that the fuses are the type the maker states.
Check the meter on a **known value** before you trust it: a proving unit, a known battery or a known resistor.
Set the function and range **before** the probes touch the circuit; never turn the dial while connected.
Hold the probes behind the finger guards. Keep one hand away from the circuit where you can.
Resistance, continuity and insulation tests are done on **dead** circuits only.
Do not measure in wet conditions or with wet hands.
After use, put the red lead back in V Ω, switch the meter off and put it away.

blocks.p: The current ranges of a multimeter are protected by fuses. Good meters use special **high-energy (high breaking capacity) fuses**, usually ceramic, rated for a high voltage such as 1,000 V. If the meter is wrongly connected across a supply, this fuse must break a very large current safely.

ul: Replace a blown fuse **only with the exact type** the maker states: the same current rating, voltage rating and breaking capacity.
A glass fuse from a car or a cheap fuse of the same amps can shatter or keep arcing, and the meter can explode in your hand.
Never bridge a fuse holder with wire or foil.
A blown fuse means the meter was misused: find out what happened and tell your instructor.

head: Do
Why
rows: Switch off after use; take the battery out if the meter will not be used for a long time
Saves the battery, and stops a leaking battery from damaging the meter
Replace the battery when the low-battery sign shows
A weak battery can give wrong readings
Wipe clean with a dry cloth
Dirt and moisture can make current leak across the case
Store in its case, with the leads coiled loosely, in a cool, dry place
Protects it from knocks, dust and damp; tight coils crack lead insulation
Keep it away from heavy tools and out of hot vehicles
Heat in a closed van in the Jamaican sun can damage the display, battery and accuracy
Do not drop it; if it is dropped, check it before use
A drop can crack the case or upset the readings

blocks.p: Over time, and after knocks, heat or misuse, instruments drift and read wrongly. **Calibration** compares an instrument with a more accurate standard and adjusts it if needed. Instruments are calibrated at set times (often every year, as the Centre's schedule says), and a label shows the date of the last check and when the next is due.

ul: Check the calibration label before you use an instrument. If it is **out of date**, do not use it: tag it and hand it in.
Between calibrations, check meters on known values, such as a proving unit, a check box or a known resistor.
An instrument that is damaged, has been dropped or gives doubtful readings is **tagged out of use** and reported until it has been checked.

sections.title: Recording results and checking unexpected readings

blocks.p: Write each result on the proper record **straight after** the measurement, so that it is not forgotten or mixed up. A result that is not recorded is a test that was not done.

ul: What was tested and where: the circuit, and between which points or conductors.
The **value with its unit and prefix**: 0.42 Ω, 12.3 V, 250 MΩ.
The instrument used (and its number), the range or test voltage.
The date and the name of the person who did the test.
Pass or fail against the expected value, and any notes.

head: Circuit / test
Between
Reading
Instrument
Pass?
rows: Panel ground bar to light box L2

blocks.h: When a reading is not what you expected

flow: Do not guess and do not change the reading
Check yourself: function, range, lead sockets, probe contact and prefix
Check the meter on a known value
Measure again
Work out with Ohm's law what the value should be
If it is still unexpected, record what you found and report it to your supervisor: it may be a fault

blocks.note: Never write down the value you expected instead of the value you measured, and never 'round' a fail into a pass. Honest records protect the people who will use the installation, and they protect you.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can name the units of voltage, current, resistance, power, energy and frequency, with their symbols.
I can change between mA and A, kΩ and Ω, and MΩ and kΩ.
I can use Ohm's law and the power formulas to work out and check readings.
I can work out total resistance, current and voltages in simple series and parallel circuits.
I can choose the right instrument for a measurement, with a suitable CAT rating.
I can check a meter, its leads and its fuses before use, and check it on a known value.
I can set the right function, range and sockets on a multimeter.
I can measure voltage with the meter in parallel, and current with the meter in series, safely.
I can use a clamp meter round one conductor and explain why the whole cable reads near zero.
I can read a digital display, including OL, a minus sign and prefixes.
I can read an analogue scale on any range without parallax error, and zero the ohms scale.
I can measure resistance and continuity on a dead circuit, nulling the leads.
I can check polarity on a lighting circuit and an outlet.
I can carry out an insulation resistance test safely and judge the result.
I can replace a meter fuse with the right type and look after and store instruments.
I can explain why instruments are calibrated and what to do with one that is out of date.
I can record results properly and deal with an unexpected reading.

head: Formula
Use
rows: I = V ÷ R; V = I × R; R = V ÷ I
P = V × I; P = I × I × R; P = V × V ÷ R
Reading = (scale reading ÷ scale full value) × range

terms: Ammeter
An instrument that measures current; connected in series.
Auto-ranging
A meter that chooses its own range.
CAT rating
A meter's measurement category, which shows where in an installation it can be used safely.
Clamp meter
A meter that measures current by sensing the magnetic field round one conductor, without breaking the circuit.
Calibration
Comparing an instrument with a more accurate standard, and adjusting it if needed.
Continuity
An unbroken path for current from one end of a conductor to the other.
Insulation resistance
The resistance of the insulation between conductors, or between a conductor and ground, measured in megohms.
Insulation resistance tester
An instrument that applies a high DC test voltage to measure insulation resistance on a dead circuit.
Kilowatt-hour (kWh)
The unit of electrical energy: 1 kW used for 1 hour.
Multimeter
An instrument that measures voltage, current and resistance, and often more.
Nulling the leads
Setting the meter to zero with the leads touched together, so that their resistance is not included.
Ohm's law
Current equals voltage divided by resistance: I = V ÷ R.
OL
Over limit: the value is above the range, or the path is open.
Parallax error
A reading error caused by looking at a needle from one side instead of straight on.
Parallel
Connected side by side across the same two points: the same voltage across each.
Polarity
Conductors connected to the correct terminals, with switches in the line conductor.
Proving unit
A small device that gives a known voltage, used to check that a tester works.
Range
The span of values a meter setting can measure, such as 0–20 V.
Resolution
The smallest step a display or scale can show.
Series
Connected one after another in a single path: the same current through each.
Voltmeter
An instrument that measures voltage; connected in parallel.

c1.title: A solar lighting kit on a farm near Santa Cruz
c1.text: Trainee Akeem is helping Mr Ewan Daley check a solar lighting kit in a chicken house on a farm near Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. A solar panel charges a 12 V battery, which feeds two 12 V, 10 W filament lamps connected in parallel through a switch and a fuse. Akeem is using a manual-range digital multimeter.

c2.title: A water heater that trips in Hayes
c2.text: Mrs Gayle's water heater in Hayes, Clarendon, keeps tripping the two-pole GFCI breaker that protects it. The heater is rated 3,000 W at 220 V. Electrician Mr Andre Morrison clamps one line conductor while the heater is running and reads 13.6 A. He then isolates and locks off the circuit. With the element disconnected, trainee Tanya measures its resistance as 16.2 Ω. Mr Morrison then tests the insulation between the element terminals and the metal tank at 500 V and reads 0.02 MΩ.

c3.title: Testing a new lighting circuit in a Junction shop
c3.text: Trainee Shamar and his supervisor Ms Joan Francis are testing a new lighting circuit in a shop in Junction, St Elizabeth, before it is connected to the supply. The circuit has a one-way switch, three screw-type lamp holders in metal boxes, and a grounding conductor to each box. The circuit is not connected at the panel, and it has been proved dead. On the low-resistance range, the meter's leads read 0.4 Ω when touched together.

c4.title: The meter cupboard at a Port Maria workshop
c4.text: At a maintenance workshop in Port Maria, St Mary, trainee Kimberly is sorting out the meters before a job. She finds a digital meter whose 10 A fuse has blown, and the only spare is a 10 A glass fuse from a car kit; the meter's label calls for a 10 A, 1,000 V ceramic fuse. She also finds a meter marked CAT II 300 V that a technician wants to use at a distribution panel, an analogue multimeter, and a digital meter that was left on the dashboard of the van all week.

questions.q: On DC volts, the meter reads −12.7 across the battery. What does this tell Akeem?
o: The battery is being charged the wrong way by the solar panel
The leads are reversed, and the battery is at about 12.7 V
The meter is on AC volts and the reading cannot be trusted
The battery is faulty and is giving out a negative voltage
questions.why: On DC a digital meter shows a minus sign when the red probe is on the negative side. The size of the reading is still correct: about 12.7 V, which is normal for a charged 12 V lead-acid battery at rest. Swap the probes for a positive reading.

questions.q: With both lamps on, about what total current should Akeem's meter show?
o: About 0.83 A
About 20 A
About 1.7 A
About 0.42 A
questions.why: Each lamp draws I = P ÷ V = 10 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.83 A. In parallel the branch currents add: 0.83 + 0.83 ≈ 1.7 A. Using Ohm's law first tells you what range and socket to use and whether the reading makes sense.

questions.q: With the battery disconnected, one lamp measures 1.3 Ω, yet 12 V ÷ 0.83 A gives about 14 Ω. Why the difference?
o: A lamp filament has a far lower resistance when it is cold
The meter's battery is weak, so its reading is ten times low
The lamp must be short-circuited and should be replaced
The fuse in the circuit adds about 13 Ω when the lamp is lit
questions.why: A filament's resistance rises steeply as it heats up, often to ten times or more its cold value. The 14 Ω is its resistance when lit; 1.3 Ω cold is normal. This is why the current is high for a moment when a filament lamp is switched on.

questions.q: Akeem has just measured the lamp current in the 10 A socket. What must he do before he measures the battery voltage again?
o: Leave the leads as they are and change only the dial to volts
Turn the dial to the 10 A range, which also reads volts
Remove the fuse in the meter, so no current can flow
Move the red lead back to V Ω and set the dial to DC volts
questions.why: In the current socket the meter is almost a short circuit. Touched across the battery it would blow the meter's fuse or cause an arc. Both the lead and the dial must be changed back before measuring voltage.

questions.q: From the clamp reading of 13.6 A, about how much power is the heater using?
o: About 16 W
About 0.3 kW
About 30 kW
About 3.0 kW
questions.why: P = V × I = 220 × 13.6 ≈ 2,990 W, or about 3.0 kW: the heater's rating. So the element is heating normally when it runs; the trips have another cause.

questions.q: Is Tanya's reading of 16.2 Ω what you would expect for this element?
o: Yes: a 3,000 W, 220 V element is about 16 Ω
No: a good element should read close to 0 Ω
No: a good element should read OL, an open path
No: it should be about 220 Ω, the same as the volts
questions.why: R = V × V ÷ P = 220 × 220 ÷ 3,000 ≈ 16.1 Ω, so 16.2 Ω is right. OL would mean a broken element, and almost 0 Ω a short circuit. Resistance wire changes little with temperature, so the cold reading is close to the working value.

questions.q: What does the insulation reading of 0.02 MΩ between the element and the tank show?
o: The insulation is in good condition, as it reads in megohms
The tester is faulty, because an element should read near 16 Ω
The insulation has broken down and current leaks to the tank
The tank is not grounded and needs a new grounding conductor
questions.why: 0.02 MΩ is only 20,000 Ω, far below the usual minimum of about 1 MΩ. Current is leaking from the element through damaged insulation to the grounded tank, which is enough to trip a GFCI. The element must be replaced and the circuit retested.

questions.q: Why does Mr Morrison tell Tanya to keep her hands off the terminals and the tank during the insulation test?
o: Her hands would warm the element and change the reading
The tester applies about 500 V DC, which can give a shock
The supply could come back on during the test at any time
The tank holds hot water that could scald her hands
questions.why: An insulation tester makes its own high DC test voltage, here 500 V, which can give a painful shock, and the circuit can hold a charge after the test. Keep hands off during the test and let the circuit discharge before touching it.

questions.q: The grounding conductor from the panel end to the second lamp box reads 0.9 Ω, including the leads. What is the conductor's own resistance?
questions.why: The leads add 0.4 Ω to every reading, so take it away: 0.9 − 0.4 = 0.5 Ω. Many meters can null the leads so the display shows the conductor alone. A low value like this shows the conductor is continuous.

questions.q: The insulation test reads very high from line to ground and neutral to ground, but almost 0 MΩ from line to neutral. What is the most likely cause?
o: The grounding conductor is missing from the lamp boxes
The tester's battery is flat, so it can only read zero
A lamp is still in a holder, joining line to neutral
The switch is open, so it blocks the test voltage
questions.why: A lamp's filament connects line to neutral, so with a lamp in place that pair reads almost zero although the insulation may be perfect. Remove every lamp, keep the switch closed, and test again.

questions.q: Which finding during the polarity check means the circuit must be corrected?
o: The centre contact of each lamp holder goes to the switched line
The grounding conductor is connected to every metal box
The neutral goes to the screw shell of each lamp holder
The switch is connected in the neutral, not the line
questions.why: With the switch in the neutral, the lamp goes off but the lamp holder stays live, so someone changing a lamp could get a shock. The switch must be in the line conductor; the other three findings are correct.

questions.q: With the switch closed, the continuity test along the switched line from the switch to the first lamp holder reads OL. What does this mean?
o: The conductor is sound, and OL is the normal result
A break: perhaps a loose terminal or a broken conductor
The circuit is live and the meter has detected voltage
The meter's leads need nulling before a reading can show
questions.why: On a resistance or continuity range, OL means the path is open. There is a break between the two points: a loose or missed terminal, a broken conductor or a faulty switch. Check each joint along that path, put it right and retest.

questions.q: Why must Kimberly not fit the 10 A glass car fuse in the meter?
o: A glass fuse lets the meter read current in one direction only
It would make the meter read about ten times too high
It may not break a large fault current safely and could burst
Glass fuses are only allowed in analogue meters
questions.why: The meter's ceramic high-energy fuse is made to break a very large fault current at up to 1,000 V if the meter is wrongly connected across a supply. A small glass fuse of the same amps can shatter or keep arcing, and the meter can explode. Fit only the exact type stated.

questions.q: Is the CAT II 300 V meter suitable for measuring at the distribution panel?
o: No: a panel is CAT III, so it needs a CAT III meter
Yes: 300 V is higher than 220 V, so it is safe to use there
Yes, as long as the technician wears rubber gloves
No: a CAT II meter may be used only on DC circuits
questions.why: A distribution panel is part of the fixed installation, CAT III, where voltage spikes are larger than at an outlet. The meter and its leads must be rated at least CAT III for the voltage there. The voltage figure alone is not enough.

questions.q: The technician uses the analogue meter on its 0–250 V AC range. The needle stops at 4.4 on the scale marked 0–10. What voltage does it show?
questions.why: Reading = scale reading ÷ scale full value × range = 4.4 ÷ 10 × 250 = 110 V. Reading the 0–10 scale without multiplying, or multiplying by the wrong factor, is a common mistake.

questions.q: What should Kimberly do with the digital meter that spent a week on the van's dashboard?
o: Use it as normal, since digital meters are not affected by heat
Check it on a known value, then store it in its case
Cool it in the workshop fridge so it reads correctly again
Leave it switched on overnight so that the battery recovers
questions.why: Strong heat in a closed vehicle can damage a meter's display, battery and accuracy. Check it on a known value, such as a proving unit or known resistor; if it reads wrongly, tag it out of use. Store meters in their cases in a cool, dry place.

questions.q: Three heater elements of 110 Ω each are wired in parallel across a 220 V supply. What total current do they draw?
o: 2 A
6 A
questions.why: Each element has the full 220 V across it, so each draws 220 ÷ 110 = 2 A. In parallel the branch currents add: 3 × 2 = 6 A. (Working it the other way: three 110 Ω in parallel make about 36.7 Ω, and 220 ÷ 36.7 ≈ 6 A.) 0.67 A would be the current if they were in series.

questions.q: An air-conditioner uses 1.5 kW and runs for 8 hours. How much energy does it use?
o: 9.5 kWh
12 kWh
5.3 kWh
questions.why: Energy = power × time = 1.5 kW × 8 h = 12 kWh. This is what the JPS meter counts and the bill charges for.

questions.q: Two lamps are in series on a 12 V DC board. The voltage across one lamp is 7.5 V. What should the meter read across the other?
questions.why: In a series circuit the voltages across the parts add up to the supply voltage: 12 − 7.5 = 4.5 V. Unequal voltages mean the lamps have different resistances.

questions.q: Which instrument shows how a voltage changes with time, such as the shape of the 50 Hz mains wave?
o: An oscilloscope
A tachometer
An energy meter
An insulation tester
questions.why: An oscilloscope draws the waveform on a screen, so you can see its shape, its peak value and how long each cycle takes (20 ms at 50 Hz). It is used mostly in electronics work.
